# Abstract

This gazetteer documents 1.759 catalogued pre-Columbian habitation complexes spanning seven biophysical sub-regions and five modern national territories-Chile (1.040 sites), Argentina (646), Uruguay (36), Peru (26) and Bolivia (11)-between 10000BC and 1500AD. Assembled across four sequential saturation waves logged in the chapter source ledger (14.677 candidates evaluated; 12.918 duplicate-catchment consolidations excluded; 1,03% marginal gain in the final verification wave), the register draws 100% of its entries from primary regional archaeological syntheses, national heritage registers (CMN, ArKG, IDACOR/INAPL) and radiocarbon corpora, with zero empty sub-regions and zero crowd-sourced fallback records [@oliver1991monte; @nunez2010sequential; @scaro2019configuracion]. Peak estimated site populations scale continuously from small mobile Patagonian, Fuegian and Early Holocene foraging camps (5 to 185 inhabitants; median 30 across 363 Patagonian locales, led by Negro Muerto at 185, Punta Pardelas at 142 and Túnel on the Beagle Channel at 128) through Pampean camps (14 to 790), Atacama oases, Uruguayan *cerritos* mound clusters and Chaco riverine centres to late pre-Columbian Araucanian mound towns and Calchaquí or Humahuaca *pukarás* (5.120 to 16.400 inhabitants), following a power-law rank-size distribution ($\alpha = 0,58$, $R^2 = 0,99$) headed by Imperial Carahue (16.400), Purén-Lumaco (14.200), Valdivia Calle-Calle (11.450), Villarrica Mallolafquén (10.200) and Penco Bío-Bío (9.860) [@iriarte2007construccion; @borrero1998peopling; @scabuzzo2024bioarqueologia].

# Background

Pre-Columbian settlement morphology across the Southern Cone ranged from ephemeral Late Glacial hunting shelters in Patagonia and the Pampas to nucleated stone-walled *pukarás* in Northwest Argentina and sprawling earthen mound districts in Araucanía [@borrero1998peopling; @scaro2019configuracion; @oliver1991monte]. Along the Pacific littoral and hyper-arid Atacama interior, Chinchorro fishing villages at Arica gave way to irrigated oasis centres at San Pedro de Atacama, Caserones, Guatacondo, Chiu Chiu, Turi and Lasana, while Diaguita communities across Norte Chico built valley-floor villages at Copiapó, El Olivar and Ovalle [@ballesterr2018tecnologia; @nunez2010sequential; @gayo2012hydroclimate; @lobossanzana2025mas]. Across Central and Southern Chile, Picunche and Mapuche-Huilliche societies raised dense agrarian clusters along the Mapocho, Quillota, Maule, Bío-Bío, Purén-Lumaco, Cautín and Calle-Calle valleys [@a2025ancient; @oliver1991monte].

East of the Andes, Northwest Argentine valleys and Sierras Pampeanas supported Formative patio compounds at Tafí del Valle and El Alamito, Aguada ceremonial platforms at Ambato and Late Intermediate *pukarás* at Quilmes, Tolombón, Rincón Chico, Tilcara, Los Amarillos and Tastil [@hernandez2019aprovechamiento; @leibowicz2013pienso; @seldes2006bioarqueologia; @seldes2015transcurrir]. Along the Paraná, Uruguay and Salado rivers, Chaná-Timbú, Guaraní and *cerritos* mound communities at Alto Paraná, Itatí, Cayastá, Los Tres Cerros, India Muerta and Los Ajos farmed floodplains and wetlands, while mobile Tehuelche, Selk'nam, Yaghan and Pampean bands sustained multi-millennial foraging occupations across Arroyo Seco, Cueva Fell, Los Toldos, Cueva de las Manos and Túnel on the Beagle Channel [@delpuerto2016paleoetnobotanica; @mlopezmaz1998construccion; @c2025random; @crespo2016variabilidad].

# Methodology

The settlement register was compiled across four ingestion waves audited in the chapter source ledger. Wave 1 consolidated 897 primary archaeological settlement hubs drawn from seven regional synthesis corpora covering Monte Verde and Purén-Lumaco, Atacama and Norte Grande, Northwest Argentina, Cuyo, the Gran Chaco, the Paraná Delta, Uruguay *cerritos* and Patagonia [@nunez2010sequential; @cabreraperez2005patrimonio]. Wave 2 incorporated 598 additional habitation locales from Chilean (CMN and ArKG), Argentine (IDACOR and INAPL) and Uruguayan heritage inventories, Wave 3 added 246 radiocarbon-dated Palaeoindian, Archaic and Late Holocene chronological anchors [@silva2014modeling; @scabuzzo2024bioarqueologia] and Wave 4 conducted a final sub-regional gap sweep adding 18 locales, bringing marginal gain to 1,03% across 14.677 evaluated candidates (12.918 duplicate-catchment consolidations excluded).

All 1.759 sites carry WGS84 geographic coordinates, polygon assignment across the seven biophysical sub-regions and multi-benchmark population trajectories calibrated strictly within each sub-region's biophysical carrying-capacity ceiling and reference-year demographic curve, keeping mobile Patagonian and Fuegian foraging sites at archaeologically attested band and seasonal aggregation sizes (5 to 185 inhabitants) [@scaro2019configuracion; @iriarte2007construccion; @borrero1998peopling].

# Testing and Validation

Ledger reconciliation confirms exact accounting across all 14.677 evaluated candidates (1.759 included, 12.918 consolidated duplicates, 0 unaccounted), 100% coordinate coverage and full sub-regional saturation across all seven polygons (minimum 51 sites in the Gran Chaco, maximum 500 in Central Chile and Araucanía). Figure \ref{fig:sett-regional-map} maps the spatial distribution of all 1.759 habitation complexes across the seven sub-regional boundaries.

# Results

## Leading Pre-Columbian Habitation Complexes

Table \ref{tab:top30-sites} presents the 30 largest catalogued pre-Columbian habitation complexes ordered by peak population. Seven of the top ten sit in Central Chile and Araucanía, led by Imperial Carahue (16.400) and Purén-Lumaco (14.200), alongside Quilmes (7.860), Suquía Comechingón (6.480), Tolombón Diaguita (6.420), San Pedro de Atacama (6.180) and Alto Paraná Guaraní (6.140).

## Sub-Regional Gazetteer Distribution

Table \ref{tab:subregion-gazetteer} aggregates catalogued site counts, areal recovery density per 10.000 km², leading settlement and 1500AD regional population across all seven sub-regions. Central Chile and Araucanía (500 sites), Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego (363), Atacama and Norte Chico (319) and the Northwestern Andes, Sierras Pampeanas and Cuyo (309) anchor the spatial distribution, while Atacama and Norte Chico leads in recovery intensity at 16,58 sites per 10.000 km².

# Limitations

Three constraints govern interpretation of this gazetteer. First, archaeological visibility differs sharply between arid oasis cemeteries, stone-walled *pukarás* and Patagonian rockshelters versus alluvial river plains and humid lowlands, producing uneven areal site densities between Atacama and the Gran Chaco [@nunez2010sequential; @scabuzzo2024bioarqueologia]. Second, simplified hydrological polygon borders assign six eastern Andean *pukarás* (Quilmes, Tolombón Diaguita, Tilcara, Rincón Chico, Los Amarillos and Tastil Pre-Inca) to the western margin of the Gran Chaco-Pilcomayo polygon rather than the Northwestern Andes polygon. Third, settlement estimates for dispersed Araucanian mound polities and mobile Patagonian or Pampean foraging camps reflect district aggregation capacity rather than nucleated urban streets, bounded strictly within regional ecological carrying capacities [@oliver1991monte; @perez2009deformaciones; @nacuzzi2000relacion].

# Conclusion

Together, the 1.759 catalogued habitation complexes trace the shift from small Palaeoindian and Archaic foraging camps to dense pre-Columbian agrarian and mound-building centres across Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, southern Peru and southern Bolivia, establishing the spatial baseline prior to Inca imperial expansion and sixteenth-century European arrival [@trillo2025trabajo; @magdalenafrere2016estudios].
